notes.title: The Qualities of a Protégé
notes.summary: Dr. Angel taught the 10 qualities of a protege, from being a master listener to honoring your mentor, with the ping pong coach illustration on strengthening strengths instead of fixing weaknesses. A bonus teaching covered liars, truth, and accuracy: how to tell deliberate deceivers from people who are simply inaccurate, and why accuracy has its place. The class also named guilt and shame as what keeps a protege from approaching a mentor, and pointed ahead to the next teaching, Discovering the Power of Purpose.
notes.full_text:
# NCU Class Notes — Thursday, October 29, 2026
Teacher: Dr. Angel. Topic: The Qualities of a Protégé.
(Summarized from the class transcript Ralph shared after class. Class ran past 7:26 p.m.; Ms. Lynn took attendance and closed in prayer.)

## The 10 qualities

1. **Be a master listener.** Total focus on the mentor: no calls, no texting, no reading. Part of listening is writing it down. A short pencil is better than a long memory. Never go before wisdom without pencil and paper.
2. **Learn and discern from an imperfect mentor.** No mentor is perfect in any of their roles. Extract good information from an imperfect source. You will not agree with every book in the program, and that is on purpose.
3. **Clearly define what success means to you.** Success is the fulfillment of a worthy goal. For the believer the heart of it is doing and fulfilling the will of God. Knowing your definition points you to your assignment and, in this context, to the right mentor: find a mentor who has developed success in the direction you want to go.
4. **The protégé pursues and chooses the mentor.** If the mentor chooses the protégé, that is control, not mentorship. The proof of your desire to grow is in your pursuit. The protégé decides how close he gets and how fast he grows. Do not let a mentor seeming out of reach put you off; they are human. A regular voice in your life carries a level of mentorship whether you planned it or not.
5. **Decide what you want to learn.** Set immediate goals: 90 day goals, one to two year goals, long term goals. Goals give focus, and people keep working at what they see growth in. And learn the 11th commandment: blessed are the flexible.
6. **Give your mentor feedback.** It helps the mentor recognize your filter: your thoughts, heart, and motivation. Tell them whether they are helping you or not.
7. **Never regret what you share with your mentor.** It is a personal relationship; unload wrong thoughts and let the mentor correct perspective. The mentor keeps what the protégé shares confidential, but the mentor's teaching may be passed on to others. You cannot move into your tomorrow with yesterday's information.
8. **Everyone has a weakness; a good mentor strengthens strengths.** A mentor concentrates on your strengths and develops them toward genius. A manipulator focuses on your weakness to keep you under. (Illustration: the Chinese ping pong coach, asked about weaknesses: "We ignore their weakness. Strengthen the strengths.")
9. **Be willing to invest in the relationship.** People are like elevators, they take you up or down; invest in the ones who take you up. Relationship costs time and expectation, and honor.
10. **Honor your mentor.** Honor their place in your life. It does not have to be money: sharing their words is honoring, showing up when they teach is honoring, influencing someone else with what they taught you is honoring. That is kingdom.

## Bonus teaching: liars, truth, and accuracy
- Everyone lies in the small sense (saying "I'm fine" when they are not); distinguish deliberate deceivers, who are few and not to be trusted, from people who are simply inaccurate or speaking from their perception.
- Never confront a liar. Take note of what they showed you and move forward; confronting just trains them to deceive better.
- Accuracy is a real gift and the world needs it, but it has its place: essential in a courtroom, less important over coffee with a friend. Not everyone inaccurate is a liar, and not everything accurate is the whole truth; perception shapes reports (50 people, same sunset, 50 descriptions).
- The Bible is the ultimate truth; a doctor's report can be honest and still not be the final word (testimony shared of a friend healed of kidney cancer after prayer and a 40 day fast).

## Also from class
- Guilt and shame will hinder a protégé from choosing and approaching a mentor; dropping them brings discernment.
- Next teaching coming: "Discovering the Power of Purpose," then goal setting. Classes run Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday.
- NCU is reviewing and changing curriculum this year.
- Ms. Lynn closed in prayer, including prayer for help with reaction papers, dissertations, and theses.

## Follow-ups involving Ralph
- Dr. Angel asked Ralph about AI help: she is looking forward to seeing some AI canvas and marketing work, asked him to tell her what he wants and send it over, and said they still need to talk and will talk tomorrow (Fri Oct 30). She plans to combine it with other business.
- A classmate asked Ralph to email her the thing he posted on Facebook so she can use it in her dissertation; Ralph said "Feel free to." (Open: the email itself.)
- After class Ralph told the group what Muse did today: cleaned up and unpublished about 500 YouTube videos, scanned his Facebook posts, downloaded the songs, posted them to YouTube with written descriptions, and started the TikTok account the same way.

notes.title: Honor (Student Notes)
notes.summary: Fill in the blank student notes for the Honor teaching, in Minister Lynn's voice. It opens with 'Honor is the ____ of the Kingdom,' works through what the Bible says about honor (about 146 mentions in the KJV, roughly 355 with related words), five women and eight men God honored, the difference between honor and respect (Kavod, glory), and Dr. Murdock's wisdom keys on honor, including 'Everywhere you sow honor you reap favor.' Received from Ralph on November 19, 2026. The notes themselves carry no class date.
notes.full_text:
Honor Student Notes

Honor is the ____________________ of the Kingdom

We honor others not because they necessarily deserve it but because of who we are.

What does the Bible say about honor..?

If you do a word search in The Bible on the word "honor" you will see it is mentioned approximately 146 times in the KJV, however words relating to honor such as honorable etc would bring the total to roughly 355 times. The Biblical meaning of the word, "honor" is "profound respect, high esteem and the recognition of inherent value or worth." According to AI.

Throughout the Bible we see that God commands honor. The first time we see this is in the 10 Commandments and number 5. "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee." (Exodus 20:12.)

We are also commanded to honor those older than us. "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the Lord." (Leviticus 19:32.) and, "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren; The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity." (1 Tim 5:1-2.)

I think we can agree that honor is a big thing to God. My Pastor Dr Murdock says, "Honor will get you further than genius." I agree. Honor has tangible rewards. If we look at the 5th Commandment the reward for obeying your parents (obeying is an act of honor) says that, "It will go well with you in the land." In (Proverbs 22:4) we see, "By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and honour, and life." Honor brings life.

5 women that God honored. Please look up the Scripture and write it next to each one.

1. Mary the Mother of Jesus
2. Mary Magdalene
3. The woman at Samaria
4. The woman with the issue of blood
5. The woman who adorned Jesus feet with perfume

What about men that God honored..?

- Abraham. God honored Abraham for his profound faith, choosing him to be the father of many nations and promising to bless the world through him.
- Noah. God honored Noah's righteousness and obedience by preserving him and his family through the great flood, saving them from the coming destruction.
- Moses. Despite his own feelings of inadequacy, God honored Moses by using him to lead the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, performing great miracles and establishing a covenant.
- David. Honored for his heart after God's own, David was a brave king and warrior, known for his strength and sincerity, though he also had his failures.
- Elijah. God honored the prophet Elijah by empowering him to perform mighty acts and by taking him to heaven in a chariot of fire.
- Elisha. As Elijah's successor, God honored Elisha with miracles and continued his prophetic work for Israel.
- Joseph. God honored Joseph for his faithfulness in a life of betrayal and hardship, which ultimately led him to a position of power in Egypt.
- Cornelius. A Gentile centurion, God honored Cornelius for his piety, prayer, and generosity, and used him to bring the Gospel to the Gentiles.

What is the difference between honor and respect..? Respect focuses on what someone has done, honor focuses on the position they carry. In Hebrew the word, "Honor" is Kavod which means glory. The word, "Honor" originates from the Latin word, "honos," the god of war.

Until we receive we have nothing to give so how do we receive honor from God..? (Hebrews 11:6) explains, "But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him."

Why is honor so important not only to God but to our very lives..? Honor and morals are very closely linked. Honor is our guide to living right. You might say that a person displays valor, honesty, empathy, compassion these are characteristics of honor. You can easily tell a person of honor, they do what is right behind closed doors when no one is watching, not just in public.

Who do you show honor to..? ____________________________________________________________

Who shows you honor..? __________________________________________________________________

Wisdom Keys of Dr Murdock on Honor

"Continual honor guarantees eventual access." Example I honored my Pastor Dr Murdock for years before he invited me to work for him which granted me access to him that others didn't have.

Who would you like access to..? __________________________________________________

"When you learn honor you have learned the secret to life." All promotion comes from honor.

"Everywhere you honor you will succeed. Everywhere you dishonor you will fail." Example - my gardener story.

"Who you honor reveals who you are."

"Honor creates access faster than genius"

My favorite one that I live my life by. "Everywhere you sow honor you reap favor. Everywhere there is favor there is Money."

"Honor does not reveal the value of another. Honor reveals YOUR value of another." I said earlier we honor because of who we are not who they are.

"Honor has a fragrance." What does that mean..? I personally am drawn to people who show me honor. You call me Ma'am or Minister Lynn or Lady Lynn you get my attention. You call me Miss or Lynn or sis you get less of my attention. (present company exempt.)

"Honor is earth's highest currency."

"Honor is not what a culture defines it to be. Honor is what God defines it to be." Example in the Chinese, Japanese and Korean cultures honor is when children of all ages from toddlers to adults will kneel and kiss the feet of their parents anywhere, anytime. They bow to their elders or bosses. Depending on the relationship and seniority depends on the depth of the bow.

"I know your Wisdom when I observe who you honor."

Do you honor someone's time by always being early or do you dishonor their time by always being late..?

Church - Jesus and The Holy Spirit arrive on time, what is your excuse for being late..?

The value you put on someone's time whether it be a face to face chat, a phone call or whatever tells me all I need to know about you.

Honoring your boss at work.

Do you honor your boss..? ________________________________________

How..? __________________________________________________________________________________________________

What if I told you that taking an extra "quick" 5 mins at lunch was dishonoring.

What if I told you that "borrowing" a pen or paperclip or photocopying your own personal documents on the work photocopier was dishonoring..?

What if I told you taking personal calls and/or scrolling your socials during work hours was dishonoring..? Break times excluded.

What if I told you that not carrying out your bosses instructions to the letter was dishonoring..? If I asked you to go buy me 5 boxes of cards. You went to the store and you saw they had an offer on, 6 for $10 and you see that 5 would cost $10.50 what would you buy me..? ________________________________________

Why..? ________________________________________

"True honor is never forgotten. Nor is dishonor."

What kind of experience do you want to be known for..? __________________________________________________________________

Do you live a life of honor..? ________________________________________

In what way..? __________________________________________________________________

notes.title: Honor When You Know Too Much
notes.summary: Ralph's article on the honor class discussion, sent in chat November 19, 2026. What we know about a person does not outweigh what God knows about them; discernment and honor can exist at the same time; honoring a person is not approving everything they do. Truth without contempt, discernment without condemnation, boundaries without disrespect.
notes.full_text:
Honor When You Know Too Much

There are people we find easy to honor. They have earned our respect, their character is evident, and we appreciate what they bring into our lives. Then there are others. We know some of their history. We have seen things, heard things, or experienced things that make extending honor a little more difficult.

That is where a recent class discussion on honor really got my attention.

One thought stood out: what I know about a person does not outweigh what God knows about that person. What I see in them today does not tell me everything God sees in their future. I may have reasons for being cautious. I may recognize behavior that concerns me. But I don’t get to make my personal assessment the standard by which someone is worthy of dignity.

That doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine. It doesn’t mean abandoning discernment or ignoring boundaries. It means understanding that discernment and honor can exist at the same time.

I was asked whether I would still honor someone while I was trying to figure out who they were. My answer was yes. Getting to know someone is a process of discovery, not a judgment about their worth. I’m learning how to relate to them, whether there might be an opportunity for friendship, business, or ministry. Their relationship with God is not mine to manage.

That distinction matters. Sometimes we close a door before we have even discovered why God may have brought someone across our path. We decide who they are based on what we know, and miss the possibility of what we don’t know.

The discussion also touched on titles and recognition. Some people are comfortable being given a place of honor; others would rather sit quietly among everyone else. Yet they may accept that recognition because they understand it is an expression of respect from those offering it. Honor isn’t always about what we want to receive. Sometimes it is about respecting what someone else is trying to communicate.

And there is a difference between honoring a person and approving everything they do. Honor does not require blind agreement, false familiarity, or surrendering healthy boundaries. It asks something more difficult of us: to treat people with dignity even when our personal feelings make that inconvenient.

I keep coming back to this. It is easy to honor someone when we believe they deserve it. The real test comes when we know enough to hesitate. Do we let what we know become the limit of what God might still do?

God never asked us to make honor conditional on our own terms. He calls us to look beyond our first impressions and remember that every person we encounter has a story we do not fully know.

Jesus demonstrated that kind of regard for people throughout His ministry. He saw beyond the labels others placed on them. He met people with truth, but He did not reduce them to their worst moment.

That is the balance worth learning. Truth without contempt. Discernment without condemnation. Boundaries without disrespect.

The way, the truth, and the life are not just words we say. They shape how we see and treat the people standing in front of us.

Who we honor reveals something about how we see others. And sometimes the person who is hardest for us to honor reveals the most about what still needs to change in us.

— RockDogPoet

#Honor #Character #FaithInAction #ChristianLiving #Discernment #WayTruthLife

notes.title: Christian Counseling (Study Guide)

notes.full_text:
# Christian Counseling — Study Guide

**Class:** Christian Counseling, New Covenant University
**Date:** Friday, November 20, 2026
**Teacher:** Dr. Lenado D. Todd, D.C.L.
**Class length:** 75 minutes, online

Dr. Angel Crites introduced Dr. Todd as an ex-student from last year or the year before, saying, "what he doesn't know about counselling is not worth knowing. When he speaks, I listen." Dr. Todd did his bachelor's and master's in Christian counseling with NCU. He works with young people, families, and people dealing with anger and conflict.

## A note before you read

This study guide has two kinds of material in it, and they are marked so you can tell them apart.

**What Dr. Todd actually taught in the recorded part of the class** is written out in the sections below. The class transcript ends in the middle of his teaching, when his connection dropped. Someone in the class said, "I think Dr. Todd just got himself raptured," and mentioned weather in the Bahamas. The last thing he taught before the connection dropped was the iceberg picture of anger. Everything after that point in this guide comes from the printed student notes and worksheet, not from his spoken words, and it is marked that way.

**Material from the printed student notes and worksheet** (DRL Christian Counseling Student Notes and DRL Student Worksheet) is marked **[From the printed notes]** wherever it goes beyond what Dr. Todd covered in the recorded portion. That includes the six counseling approaches, the ABC model, making a plan, case conceptualization, measurable goals, the crisis response teaching, the seven stages of crisis intervention, and the handoff and follow-up steps. Dr. Todd did not teach those parts in the recorded portion of the class. They are in the printed notes, so they are in this guide, but they are not presented here as things he said out loud in class.

Nothing in this guide invents teaching Dr. Todd did not give. Where the notes go beyond the transcript, this guide says so.

## Administrative note

At the start of class Dr. Angel made an administrative announcement that a student had been asked to leave the university. She asked whether anyone had communication from Miss Leslie Arden. One student said only what she saw in the group, nothing else. Dr. Angel asked that any communication be sent directly to her.

## Summary

Christian counseling brings biblical wisdom into helping people. It starts with a person's dignity, because every person is made in the image of God. A mistake may explain why somebody came for help, but it can never tell you the whole story about who they are. The counselor listens well, speaks honestly about what a person did while still treating them with respect, bears burdens with people, and only brings prayer and Scripture in with the person's permission. The class worked through ten qualities of a counselor, how confidentiality and boundaries work, and the four parts of a session, using the case of Jordan, a 20-year-old who was corrected in front of his classmates and stopped attending class. The printed notes carry the teaching further, into six counseling approaches, the ABC model, making a plan with the client, and crisis response and follow-up.

## 1. Faith, dignity, and permission

### Every person is made in the image of God

Genesis 1:27: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."

A person's dignity comes from being made in God's image. That is where dignity starts, and it does not change because of what a person did. When someone tells you something they regret, you can speak honestly about what they did and still treat them with respect. Begin with a person's dignity. A mistake may explain why somebody came for help, but it can never tell you the whole story about who they are.

### Bear one another's burdens

Galatians 6:2: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."

Bearing burdens can mean sitting with someone in a painful moment and helping them figure out what support they need. It is not always fixing the problem. Sometimes it is staying present while the person works through it.

### Active listening

Put the phone away. Give the person your full attention. They will see it if you glance at your phone. Listening is part of bearing the burden. A person who feels heard will tell you more of what is really going on.

### Bring prayer and Scripture only with permission

Ask: "Would you like prayer or scripture to be a part of our conversation today?" If the person says yes, ask what would be helpful. If the person says no, say, "Okay, of course, no problem." Do not push it.

Give the person room to talk about their faith in their own words, including doubt or painful experiences. Let them say it the way they would say it. You do not have to correct their language before you have heard what they mean.

## 2. Ten qualities of a counselor

Galatians 6:1: "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."

Paul pairs gentleness with how honestly we look at ourselves. Restoring someone takes meekness, and it takes remembering that you could be tempted too. The ten qualities, in the order Dr. Todd taught them:

1. **Patience.** Give the person time. Recognize small steps forward. Progress is not always fast, and small steps count.
2. **Good listening.** Hear them out. Verify that you understood what they said before you move on.
3. **Compassion.** Let your words and your actions show that their pain matters to you.
4. **Non-judgmental attitude.** Talk plainly about harmful behavior while protecting the person's dignity. Stay neutral. You can name what was wrong without making the person feel worthless.
5. **Commit to ongoing study.** Learning never stops. Consult reliable sources. Ask for guidance. Do not be ashamed to say you need to learn more.
6. **Empathy.** Understand how the situation feels from their side, not just from yours.
7. **Discretion.** Be careful with what people tell you. What is said in session stays in session, EXCEPT you must report it if they want to kill themselves or kill somebody else.
8. **Encouragement.** Name something specific they did well, something they can build on. For example, forgiving someone was big. Be specific, not general.
9. **Self-awareness.** Notice when your own experience makes you jump to conclusions. Your experience may not have ended the way theirs will. What happened to you is not automatically what will happen to them.
10. **Authenticity.** Be real about what you know, what you can offer, and what you can't help with. Do not overextend yourself, and do not say the wrong thing just to fill the silence.

### Class discussion: pick one strength and one to work on

Dr. Todd had everyone in the class pick one strength from the ten and one to work on.

One student said her strength is compassion, "showing genuine concern for their pain." Her weakness, she said, is that she would tell people how to fix themselves: "I will tell you the scripture and the verse and where to go and how to do it and get on with it. That's my weakness."

Another student said her strength is pattern recognition and body language, listening for patterns and repetition in what a person says and how they carry themselves. Her weakness is listening itself, staying in the moment, active listening.

A student later asked what number four was. Dr. Todd answered: "Patience."

## 3. Confidentiality and boundaries

Proverbs 11:13: "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter."

Explain your role, what gets recorded, who can access it, and when safety or reporting rules may require involving someone else, BEFORE the person shares sensitive information. Do not wait until after they have told you something private. Give the person time to ask questions about how it works.

Suggested wording from the class: "Before we begin, let me explain how your information is handled, who may have access to it, and the situation when I may need to involve somebody else, for safety or because a reporting requirement..."

If the person knows you through church or school, talk about how you will handle contact outside sessions. They need to know how you will act when you see them somewhere else.

With young people, use language they can understand, and follow the procedure for your setting.

When writing notes, separate three things: what the person told you, what you saw or heard yourself, and what you agreed to do. Keep agreements you make. Protect access to records. Do not leave notes lying around where someone can pick them up.

If a concern goes beyond your training or role, get supervision, get help, and connect the person with someone who can provide the care that is needed. Knowing your limits is part of the work, not a failure at it.

## 4. The Jordan case and the four-part session

Jordan is 20 years old. One day Jordan was corrected in front of his classmates. Since then Jordan stopped attending class. Jordan tells us: "Everybody thinks I'm a failure. I get angry just thinking about going back to that class."

What Jordan told us: he felt degraded. Guilt and shame are in this too.

What to find out:

- What was said when Jordan was corrected.
- What Jordan noticed about the classmates' reactions. Nobody stood by him. "Everybody thinks he's a failure."
- Whether something similar has happened before.
- What Jordan wants help with. Maybe help dealing with the correction. Maybe help getting back to class. Maybe why the adult corrected him that way.

### The four parts of a session

1. **Open the session.**
2. **Gather information.**
3. **Discuss the concern.**
4. **Close with next step.**

James 1:19: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath."

Proverbs 18:13: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him."

### Open with an open question

"Jordan, what would you like help with today?" Like a doctor asking what is wrong. Do not prescribe before you have heard what the problem is.

### Gather information with open questions

"What went through your mind when you were corrected?" An open question invites the person to say more.

A closed question confirms facts: "Have you attended class since then?" That kind of question checks something specific. It does not open the conversation up, it settles a fact.

Give them time to answer. Watch tone, posture, and facial expression. A weird expression can close the door. If Jordan goes quiet, pause and ask, "What is going on through your mind right now?" Let him tell you what the silence means. Do not guess for him.

### Paraphrase what you heard

"Being corrected in front of everybody sounds embarrassing." A paraphrase checks one part of what you heard, and it lets the person hear their own story reflected back with care.

### The iceberg

Anger is what people see above the water, but it is not the actual problem. Embarrassment underneath may be the actual problem. Jordan did not talk about it. He just reacts. That is where the teaching stopped.

**The transcript ends here. Dr. Todd's connection dropped in the middle of this teaching, before he finished the Jordan case. What follows in sections 5 through 8 comes from the printed student notes and worksheet, not from the recorded portion of the class.**

---

## 5. Six counseling approaches

**[From the printed notes]**

1. **Person-centered.** Empathy and acceptance help the client explore their experience. The counselor gives the person room to say what is really going on, without rushing to fix it.
2. **Holistic.** Considers the whole picture: physical, emotional, social, vocational, intellectual, and spiritual. A problem in one area often touches the others.
3. **Strengths-based.** Draws on the client's abilities, resources, and previous successes. What has worked for them before? Who can they lean on?
4. **Cognitive behavioral.** Explores how beliefs influence feelings and actions. What a person believes about what happened shapes how they feel and what they do next.
5. **Solution-focused.** Uses a preferred future and small signs of progress. How would the person know things were improving? What small step would show it?
6. **Existential.** Explores meaning, identity, values, and responsibility. What does this mean to the person? Who do they understand themselves to be? What are they responsible for?

## 6. The ABC model and making a plan

**[From the printed notes]**

### The ABC model

- **A is the activating event.** What happened.
- **B is the belief or interpretation.** What the person thinks the event means.
- **C is the consequences.** What the person feels and does afterward.

With Jordan, start by separating what happened in class from what Jordan believes others thought about it. Acknowledge the embarrassment and the anger. Ask what Jordan saw or heard, what Jordan is predicting, and what else may be contributing. If there is a pattern of mistreatment, that information matters when deciding what support is appropriate.

Romans 12:2: "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." Transformation connects with renewing the mind, which is what the B in the ABC model is about: how we interpret what happened.

Ephesians 4:26: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Anger itself is not the sin. How we respond when we are angry is what matters.

### Making a plan with the client

Clarify the concern, build trust, and check your first impressions. Gather relevant information and identify supports. Agree on what the client wants to change and what action they are willing to try. Clarify what each person will do. At the end of the session, summarize the agreement and decide when to review it.

A case conceptualization is a working explanation of how the client's concerns fit together. Check it with the client and update it when new information changes your understanding. At follow-up, review what happened and decide whether to continue, adjust the plan, conclude, or seek additional support.

### Setting a measurable goal

A useful goal names what the client will try, when they will try it, and how they will review it. For the worksheet exercise, consider a step Jordan sees as safe and manageable. A follow-up question should help Jordan describe what happened and what support would make the next step easier.

Proverbs 21:5: "The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want." Diligent planning brings results. Careful planning, not rushing, is the point.

## 7. Crisis response and follow-up

**[From the printed notes]**

### Recognizing a shift in priority

In the next part of the case, Jordan says, "After what happened, I've been thinking about hurting myself tonight." The word "tonight" makes immediate safety the priority. Respond calmly, take the disclosure seriously, and follow the crisis procedures for your setting. Ask directly about suicide when indicated and promptly involve appropriate support. Activate local emergency response if danger appears imminent.

### Seven stages of crisis intervention (Roberts-Ottens model)

1. Assess immediate danger and needs.
2. Establish rapport.
3. Identify the main concern and trigger.
4. Explore feelings.
5. Identify safe coping options and supports.
6. Implement the action plan.
7. Arrange follow-up.

Several of these steps can happen together. They are not always one at a time in order.

### Handoff and follow-up

Explain the next step and involve the person designated to help. When safe, maintain contact while arranging the handoff. Confirm that the receiving person has accepted responsibility for the next step. Record what was disclosed, what was done, and who received the handoff. Confirm who will follow up and when. Offer spiritual support with permission alongside the safety response.

Definitions from the printed notes:

- **Precipitating event:** what triggered the crisis.
- **Lethality assessment:** an evaluation of danger to life.
- **Performance indicator:** an observable sign that a planned step happened.
- **Disaster response:** when an event affects many people, teams coordinate safety, practical help, and ongoing support.

Psalm 34:18: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." God is near to people who are hurting.

Colossians 4:6: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man." Gracious speech, including when a situation calls for a clear and direct response.

## 8. All the verses in this study guide

- Genesis 1:27: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."
- Galatians 6:2: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ."
- Galatians 6:1: "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."
- Proverbs 11:13: "A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter."
- James 1:19: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath."
- Proverbs 18:13: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him."
- Romans 12:2: "And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God." **[From the printed notes]**
- Ephesians 4:26: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." **[From the printed notes]**
- Proverbs 21:5: "The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want." **[From the printed notes]**
- Psalm 34:18: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." **[From the printed notes]**
- Colossians 4:6: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man." **[From the printed notes]**

## 9. Worksheet questions with answers

All 22 numbered items from the DRL Student Worksheet, with the blanks filled in.

**1.** According to Genesis 1:27, every person is made in the **image** of God.

**2.** Galatians 6:2 calls us to bear one another's **burdens**.

**3.** Before introducing prayer or Scripture, ask the client's **permission**.

**4. The ten qualities of a counselor:**
- **4a.** Give the client time and recognize gradual progress. **Patience.**
- **4b.** Hear the full concern and verify your understanding. **Good listening.**
- **4c.** Show genuine concern for the client's pain. **Compassion.**
- **4d.** Address behavior while preserving dignity. **Non-judgmental attitude.**
- **4e.** Keep learning and consult reliable sources. **Ongoing study.**
- **4f.** Understand the client's perspective and feelings. **Empathy.**
- **4g.** Protect private information and records. **Discretion.**
- **4h.** Name an effort or strength the client can build on. **Encouragement.**
- **4i.** Recognize how your own reactions affect the conversation. **Self-awareness.**
- **4j.** Speak honestly about what you know and can offer. **Authenticity.**

**5.** Proverbs 11:13 connects trustworthiness with **discretion**.

**6.** Before sensitive disclosures, explain confidentiality and its **limits**.

**7. The four parts of a session:**
- **7a.** First, **open** the session.
- **7b.** Second, gather **information**.
- **7c.** Third, **discuss** the concern.
- **7d.** Fourth, **close** the session with next steps.

**8.** James 1:19 teaches us to be quick to **hear** and slow to speak.

**9.** "Before you offer advice, give the person a chance to hear their own story **reflected back** with care."

**10.** A paraphrase checks one statement. A **summary** brings several points together.

**11. The six approaches:**
- **11a.** Empathy, acceptance, and genuineness help the client explore their experience. **Person-centered.**
- **11b.** Considers physical, emotional, social, vocational, intellectual, and spiritual factors. **Holistic.**
- **11c.** Draws on abilities, resources, and previous successes. **Strengths-based.**
- **11d.** Explores how beliefs influence feelings and actions. **Cognitive behavioral.**
- **11e.** Uses a preferred future and small signs of progress. **Solution-focused.**
- **11f.** Explores meaning, identity, values, and responsibility. **Existential.**

**12. The ABC model, applied to Jordan:**
- **12a.** A stands for **activating event**. What happened to Jordan: Jordan was corrected in front of his classmates.
- **12b.** B stands for **belief**. What Jordan concluded: everybody thinks he is a failure.
- **12c.** C stands for **consequences**. How Jordan felt and responded: he gets angry just thinking about going back to that class, and he stopped attending class.

**13.** Romans 12:2 connects transformation with renewing the **mind**.

**14.** A case **conceptualization** is a working explanation of how a client's concerns fit together.

**15.** Proverbs 21:5 connects diligent **planning** with results.

**16.** "A counseling goal becomes useful when the client can say what they'll try, when they'll try it, and what they'll look for **in review**." (What they will look for when they review it: whether the step happened, how it went, and what support would make the next step easier.)

**17. Worked example: one measurable goal for Jordan, and one follow-up question.**

Measurable goal: "Jordan will attend the first fifteen minutes of the class on Monday morning, sit near the door, and leave at the break if he needs to. He will tell the counselor afterward how it went."

Why this works as a goal: it names what Jordan will try (attend the first fifteen minutes), when he will try it (Monday morning), and how they will review it (he tells the counselor afterward how it went). The step is one Jordan sees as safe and manageable, not the whole class all at once.

Follow-up question: "What happened when you went in on Monday, and what support would make the next step easier?"

**18. The seven stages of crisis intervention (Roberts-Ottens):**
- **18a.** Stage 1. Assess immediate **danger** and needs.
- **18b.** Stage 2. Establish **rapport**.
- **18c.** Stage 3. Identify the main concern and **trigger**.
- **18d.** Stage 4. Explore **feelings**.
- **18e.** Stage 5. Identify coping options and **supports**.
- **18f.** Stage 6. Implement the action **plan**.
- **18g.** Stage 7. Arrange **follow-up**.

**19.** Psalm 34:18 teaches that God is near to the **brokenhearted**.

**20.** "Let compassion steady your voice and let wisdom guide your next **step**."

**21.** One observable sign that a crisis handoff is complete: the receiving person has accepted responsibility for the next step, and who will follow up and when is confirmed.

**22a.** How would you ask permission to include prayer or Scripture? Ask, "Would you like prayer or scripture to be a part of our conversation today?" If the person says yes, ask what would be helpful. If the person says no, say, "Okay, of course, no problem," and respect the answer.

**22b.** How does paraphrasing differ from summarizing? A paraphrase checks one statement, giving the person a chance to hear that one part of their story reflected back with care. A summary pulls several points together and gives the client a chance to clarify the whole picture.

**22c.** What becomes the priority if harm may be imminent? Immediate safety. Respond calmly, take the disclosure seriously, ask directly about suicide when indicated, promptly involve appropriate support, and activate local emergency response if danger appears imminent.

notes.title: The Four Prisons of the Mind
notes.topic: The four prisons of the mind
notes.summary: Dr. Angel taught The Four Prisons of the Mind: waiting for circumstances to change before changing ourselves; waiting for more money before stewarding what we already have; letting feelings and past experiences dictate present decisions; and holding on to a victim identity instead of recognizing what God has brought us through. The class then moved to the revised reaction-paper guidelines (four questions, three to four pages): author and three main ideas, personal application, agreement or disagreement, and personal connection or changed perspective; plus submission and formatting requirements, and a closing discussion on disagreeing civilly, respecting the person, and continuing to reveal God. The class closed with a Thanksgiving prayer and an invitation to share Thanksgiving moments in the group chat.
notes.full_text:
NCU Class Notes

The Four Prisons of the Mind

Lecturer: Dr. Angel Crites

⸻

Part One: The Four Prisons of the Mind

1. Things Must Change Around Me Before I Can Change

The first prison is the belief that external circumstances must change before internal change can happen.

Dr. Angel describes how people sometimes believe a different environment will automatically produce a different life. They may rearrange their furniture, change jobs, leave a church, change relationships, divorce and remarry, or move to another city, expecting those changes to transform who they are.

But changing the surroundings does not automatically change the person.

She uses the example of someone who receives a large amount of money through the lottery. If that person continues to carry the same habits, beliefs, and approach to money, the new financial circumstances alone may not produce a lasting change. The internal patterns still need attention.

Central principle: External change does not automatically create internal transformation. Lasting change requires a change in how we think and live.

Scripture connections:

* Romans 12:2 — Be transformed by the renewing of your mind.
* Proverbs 23:7 — As a person thinks in the heart, so is that person.

2. I Must Have Money Before I Can Be Rich

The second prison is the belief that financial resources must come first before someone can change their financial future or experience a better quality of life.

Dr. Angel explains that poverty can also become a mindset, attitude, or perspective. Her point is not simply about how much money someone has. It is about how people think, what they value, and how they use what is already in their hands.

Her instruction is to begin where you are. Change your thinking now. Make a plan with what you already have rather than waiting until you have more.

Sometimes the change needed is not additional money. It may be a change in attitude, priorities, habits, or lifestyle.

Dr. Angel’s personal example

Dr. Angel describes growing up in poverty and later living differently with Dr. Kreitz. They were not wealthy, but their mindset and lifestyle had changed. Their home and the way they lived sometimes led people to assume they were rich, even though they were not.

The point was that a good life is not measured by net worth alone. Attitude, priorities, stewardship, and how we care for what we have all matter.

The shopping example

Dr. Angel discusses people who repeatedly shop clearance racks at places such as Walmart and Kmart, buying discounted items rather than saving for something they actually want or need. The pattern repeats every weekend and during major sales such as Black Friday.

Her teaching is to decide what you want, set your mind on it, and save for quality rather than buying something simply because it is on sale.

The principle is intentional purchasing. Consider usefulness, quality, durability, and whether something is genuinely needed. This does not mean everyone should buy expensive things. It means making thoughtful decisions instead of repeating an unhelpful spending cycle.

The rent-to-own example

Dr. Angel refers to rent-to-own furniture businesses such as Aaron’s. A person may eventually pay several times the original value of an item because they want it immediately rather than waiting and saving.

Sometimes patience is more affordable than immediate access.

Stewardship of the home

Dr. Angel emphasizes starting with what you have and where you are. Take care of your living space. Learn to say no to bringing things into your home that have no real value.

She makes the point that purchases cost more than money. They also take up the real estate of your home. Every item requires space and may require attention, care, or maintenance.

Our living space is a resource. We should be intentional about what we bring into it.

Think and Grow Rich

Dr. Angel introduces Think and Grow Rich by Napoleon Hill, first published in 1937 during the Great Depression.

She tells the story that Hill was not wealthy when he wrote the book and had to borrow money from friends to submit it to publishers. That particular account was not independently verified in the earlier discussion, so it remains attributed to the lecture.

The connection to the second prison is that Hill understood ideas about success before he had achieved the financial outcome himself.

An observation from our discussion:

He already knew the keys. He just had to start walking in it with what he had.

Central principle: Do not wait for more resources before learning to manage and use the resources already in your hand. Your starting point does not have to become your stopping point.

Scripture connection:

* Matthew 25:14–30 — The parable of the talents and the responsibility to steward what has been entrusted to us.

3. I Must Pay Attention to My Feelings in Order to Reach My Goals

The third prison concerns allowing feelings to determine whether we pursue our goals.

Dr. Angel acknowledges that this subject requires some care. People who have lived in toxic environments may have been taught to ignore their feelings or instincts. She is not saying that emotions should be denied or that people should become robots.

Her focus is on reaching goals. Feelings can sometimes mislead us or become a reason to stop moving forward.

There is a time and place for feelings, but they do not have to dictate our decisions.

Don’t let other people derail your purpose

Dr. Angel uses the workplace as an example. Don’t allow coworkers or other people on the job to determine the quality of your work or distract you from your responsibilities.

If someone betrays you or turns against you, don’t allow that person’s actions to consume your attention and take over your future.

Pushing past betrayal does not mean excusing wrongdoing, restoring trust automatically, or giving someone another opportunity to hurt you. It means refusing to let their actions control your direction.

She expresses the idea this way: Don’t allow yesterday’s people to crawl into tomorrow’s plans.

Sometimes we have to untie people from the dock. Not everyone from our past belongs in our future.

Jesus and the opinions of others

Dr. Angel connects this idea to Jesus and the way people identified Him by His family and hometown.

People said, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:1–6).

They thought they knew Him. They saw His background and made assumptions about who He could be.

Dr. Angel’s application is that people may remember who we were and attempt to define us by our past. They may say, “I remember when you were that,” or “I know who you are.”

But other people’s memories and opinions do not have to become the authority over our identity or future.

She also gives an example of someone who had experienced abuse and needed to understand that she was much more than the circumstances she had lived through. A person’s identity is not limited to the worst thing that happened to them.

Marriage, feelings, and daily love

Dr. Angel says that a marriage cannot be guided by emotions alone.

She shares that she loves love and the thought of being in love. She recalls a revelation involving Dr. Kreitz: find a new reason to fall in love with your spouse every single day, even if it is something small.

Marriage is not always a dramatic expression of affection. Sometimes both people are focused on responsibilities and have work to do. Love is more than a feeling. It is expressed through daily attention, appreciation, commitment, and action.

She describes her first birthday after becoming Mrs. Kreitz. Coming out of an abusive relationship, she had become accustomed to a pattern in which birthdays could involve extravagant displays of affection and love-bombing, while ordinary days included being cursed at, mistreated, or abused.

In contrast, she now had someone who consistently loved her every day.

The Lord gave her a revelation: she had someone who loved her consistently, not just on special occasions.

She had to work through the feelings that asked whether Dr. Kreitz was angry with her or whether she had done something wrong when he was not making a dramatic romantic gesture.

A healthy, stable relationship can feel unfamiliar to someone who has come out of an abusive one. Feelings may be responding to old experiences rather than what is actually happening in the present.

Emotions and vision

Dr. Angel explains that emotions can make situations seem bigger than they are. They can make something that happened twenty years ago feel as if it happened yesterday.

Past hurt can intrude on the present and interfere with our ability to see tomorrow clearly.

She connects this to the idea that if you cannot see, you have no vision. We must put the past in its proper place so that we can be present today and move toward the future.

Bitterness and forgiveness

Dr. Angel connects bitterness with the loss of vision. Holding on to what someone did can keep us emotionally tied to the past.

The person who hurt us may never apologize. They may never acknowledge what they did or care whether we forgive them.

Forgiveness cannot depend on their response.

We can forgive, release the bitterness, and give ourselves permission to move forward. This does not mean pretending the wrongdoing never happened, excusing abuse, automatically reconciling, or restoring trust. Forgiveness and boundaries can exist together.

Think on these things

Dr. Angel quotes Philippians 4:8 from the King James Version:

“Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, if there be any praise, think on these things.”

She repeats the instruction: “Think on these things.”

The application is that we cannot always control what happens or what memories come to mind, but we can become intentional about what we continually give our attention to.

This is not denying painful realities. It is choosing where our thoughts are directed rather than allowing old wounds to occupy our minds indefinitely.

Central principle: Feelings provide information, but they do not have to control our decisions. Emotional discipline is not emotional denial. Don’t let temporary reactions or old wounds govern present decisions and future purpose.

Victory does not mean pretending you are never down. It means not surrendering your direction simply because you are down.

Scripture connections:

* Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:1–6 — Jesus and the assumptions people made about Him.
* 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 — The character and actions of love.
* 1 John 4:18 — Perfect love and fear.
* Philippians 3:13–14 — Pressing forward rather than remaining fixed on what is behind.
* Proverbs 29:18 — The importance of vision.
* Ephesians 4:31–32 — Putting away bitterness and practicing forgiveness.
* Romans 12:18–19 — Living peaceably where possible and leaving judgment to God.
* Philippians 4:8 — Directing our thoughts toward what is true, just, pure, lovely, and worthy of praise.

4. I Must Maintain My Victim Mindset to Receive the Mercy and Compassion of Others

Dr. Angel introduces the fourth prison as a particularly important one.

The belief is: “I must maintain my victim mindset to receive the mercy and compassion of others.”

She tells of speaking with a young woman who had developed a strong victim mentality. Dr. Angel says she told her:

“I’m just going to be really vulnerable with you because I can see that your victim mentality has stolen half your life and is about to steal your friends and is about to steal your opportunities.”

Dr. Angel then shares roughly half of the painful experiences she herself had gone through.

The young woman responds, “Oh my goodness, Dr. Angel, that’s a lot.”

Dr. Angel answers, “Right. But you didn’t know about it, did you?”

Her point is that the young woman had not known those experiences because Dr. Angel had not made her painful history the defining feature of her identity.

She had experienced real pain, but she had chosen not to build her life around continually displaying that pain.

Look at what God brought you through

Dr. Angel encourages students to move past the emotion attached to what happened, move past bitterness, and move past a victim mentality.

Instead of looking only at what you have been through, look at what God has brought you through.

She warns that continually seeing yourself as a victim can make you an easier target for people who want to exploit or mistreat you.

This point needs an important distinction: being victimized is never the victim’s fault. Responsibility belongs to the person who chooses to harm or exploit someone. Dr. Angel is addressing the danger of allowing victimhood to become an identity that shapes expectations, boundaries, and responses.

Christ and identity

Dr. Angel asks:

“Did God send his only son for you to be a victim? Absolutely not.”

Her point is that Christ’s sacrifice was not so that we would remain defined by our wounds, our past, or the actions of other people.

Redemption calls us beyond victimhood. We can acknowledge what happened, grieve it, seek healing, and still refuse to let it become our identity.

How you think is how you will live

Dr. Angel explains that continually thinking about what happened in the past can cause us to continue living out of that past.

Our memories can become the lens through which we interpret the present and approach the future.

She connects this to Revelation 12:11:

“And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony…”

She identifies two important parts:

* The blood of the Lamb: Our victory is rooted in what Jesus Christ has done.
* The word of our testimony: We speak not only about what happened to us, but about what God has done and how He carried us through.

Dr. Angel expresses the principle this way:

“You overcome simply by overcoming whatever overcame you. You move forward, you grew past it. I am not a victim. I am a victor.”

Overcoming does not mean the pain was imaginary or that the past no longer matters. It means the past no longer governs our identity, decisions, and future.

Declaration

“I am not defined by what happened to me. I am defined by what God has done in me and what He has brought me through. I am not a victim. I am a victor.”

Thanksgiving and a change of perspective

Dr. Angel encourages students to stop thinking only in terms of what they have gone through and begin thinking about what God has brought them through.

Instead of rehearsing only the pain, betrayal, loss, and hardship, recognize God’s faithfulness, preservation, growth, grace, and deliverance.

Gratitude does not pretend life was easy. It refuses to let hardship become the only thing we remember.

She explains that changing our attitude can change how we approach our circumstances. Rather than continually repeating, “This person hurt me,” we can acknowledge that we were hurt while also recognizing what we have come through and what we have grown through.

That recognition can become a source of strength.

Central principle: What happened to you matters, but it does not have to own the rest of your life. You do not have to remain wounded to deserve compassion. Don’t let the past write the ending. Recognize not only what you survived, but what God has grown in you along the way.

Scripture connections:

* John 3:16 — God’s love and the gift of His Son.
* Romans 8:37 — More than conquerors through Him who loved us.
* 2 Corinthians 5:17 — New creation in Christ.
* Revelation 12:11 — Overcoming through the blood of the Lamb and the word of testimony.

Part Two: Reaction Paper Guidelines

Dr. Angel transitions from the Four Prisons of the Mind to the revised reaction-paper requirements.

The previous guidelines had six questions and required two to three pages. The revised guidelines have four questions and require three to four pages.

Students who already completed papers under the previous guidelines do not need to redo them. Dr. Angel will accept both formats throughout the year.

She explains that the additional page allowance gives students more room to develop their responses.

Question 1: Author and the Book’s Three Main Ideas

Length: One paragraph, five to seven sentences.

Students must:

* Name the author.
* Describe the author’s background.
* Identify the three main ideas in the book.

Dr. Angel wants students to learn about the author and understand the perspective from which the author is writing. This includes the author’s experiences, background, and worldview.

Not every assigned author will be a Christian. That is not a reason to dismiss the book.

Dr. Angel gives the example of assigning a book about Steve Jobs in an earlier Public Communication class. Some Christian students objected because Jobs was not a Christian and used profanity.

Her response was: “Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater.”

There may be valuable ideas in someone’s work even when we disagree with aspects of their life or worldview. She pointed out that Jobs had reached and influenced a tremendous number of people and asked whether students would like to reach as many people for Jesus.

Dr. Angel has read the assigned books. She does not want students spending most of their paper retelling the book. She wants evidence that they understand the author’s three main ideas.

Educational principle: Learn to discern rather than automatically agree or disagree. Understand an author’s perspective, evaluate the ideas, and think independently.

Question 2: Personal Application

Question: How can you apply this book to your area of ministry or professional life?

Dr. Angel says generic hypothetical statements are not enough.

A weak response might say:

“In my experience as a youth pastor, I can use this main idea of the book well.”

She wants something more specific:

“This is an idea from the book I found really valuable, and I used it in this very specific instance in my life.”

Students should:

* Identify the specific idea from the book.
* Describe a real situation in which they actually applied it.
* Explain how the idea informed their response or actions.

Dr. Angel says reaction papers are more challenging because they require action in real time, not simply a statement about what someone might do in the future.

Educational principle: Demonstrate application, not intention. Learning should leave the classroom and become part of actual life, ministry, or professional practice.

Question 3: Agreement or Disagreement

Question: Do you agree or disagree with all or some of the book? What supports your stance?

Dr. Angel says that if a student agrees with every single principle in every assigned book, she will question whether the student has truly understood the material.

She intentionally selects books that include points with which she herself disagrees.

Students are expected to think critically and to be able to disagree with an idea civilly.

She uses public discourse in the United States as an example, observing that people are not always able to express disagreement respectfully. Students see examples of this in the news.

Students may strongly disagree with a book. One student in a previous year had effectively “torn it to shreds.” Dr. Angel said that was absolutely acceptable, provided the student articulated the reasons civilly.

Students should:

* Identify the specific ideas they agree or disagree with.
* Explain why they hold that position.
* Support their position with sound reasoning and evidence.
* Express their position respectfully.
* Criticize the ideas rather than personally attacking the author.

Educational principle: Critical thinking requires the freedom to disagree. Maturity means being able to do so respectfully. Students do not have to agree with the book, but they must understand it well enough to explain their disagreement.

Question 4: Personal Connection or Changed Perspective

Question: What ideas or points from the book could you relate to, or what ideas changed your perspective?

Dr. Angel explains that there are two acceptable approaches.

Option one: Personal connection

A student might explain that a point in the book connected with something experienced throughout childhood or another part of life.

The student should describe the connection between the author’s idea and the real personal experience.

Option two: Changed perspective

A student might explain that they have always approached ministry or professional life in a certain way, but the book presents a valid perspective that challenges their existing thinking.

They can identify what they previously believed, explain the alternative perspective, and describe their willingness to consider or try it.

Either approach is acceptable.

One demonstrates a meaningful personal connection. The other demonstrates intellectual growth and openness to reconsidering an established belief.

Educational principle: Show that the book genuinely engaged your thinking.

Additional Sources

Dr. Angel says students may use other sources to support their responses, including:

* Class lectures from professors.
* Teaching and guidance from mentors.
* The Bible.
* Other books and written works.

These sources can support personal application, reasoning, and responses to the author’s ideas.

Part Four: Closing Discussion – Disagreement, Courage, and Revealing God

The final discussion brings the academic guidelines back to Christian responsibility.

Dr. Angel asks:

“People that we don’t agree with, does that mean that we get to check out from and we get to excuse from revealing God to them? No.”

She makes clear that disagreement does not remove our responsibility to demonstrate God’s character to other people.

She further clarifies that we can disagree very strongly. We can challenge ideas and make our position clear.

We just cannot be rude about it.

She also says we cannot be afraid of making people angry.

Civil disagreement does not mean avoiding difficult truths, softening every position, or agreeing simply to keep everyone comfortable.

We can speak honestly, challenge an idea, and stand firmly in our convictions without disrespecting the person who holds a different view.

Central principle: Disagree with the idea. Respect the person. Do not let fear of someone’s reaction keep you from telling the truth. Continue revealing God through how you conduct yourself.

Scripture connections:

* 1 Peter 3:15 — Be prepared to give an answer, with gentleness and respect.
* Colossians 4:6 — Let your speech always be gracious.
* Matthew 5:44 — Love your enemies.

The responsibility to reveal God is not limited to people with whom we agree. Our conduct matters especially when agreement is difficult.

Overall Class Takeaways

The Four Prisons of the Mind challenge four beliefs that can keep people from moving forward:

1. Waiting for the outside world to change before changing ourselves.
2. Waiting for more money or resources before learning to use what we already have.
3. Allowing feelings and past experiences to dictate our present decisions and future direction.
4. Holding on to a victim identity instead of recognizing what God has brought us through.

The reaction-paper assignment carries a related lesson into academic work: understand what you read, apply what you learn, think critically, and be willing to disagree.

Dr. Angel’s closing discussion brings the responsibility back to our Christian walk. We do not have to agree with everyone. We do not have to avoid difficult conversations or fear making someone angry. But we must conduct ourselves in a way that continues to reveal God.

Knowledge should become practice. Conviction should remain respectful. Disagreement should not become an excuse to withdraw love. And what God has brought us through should shape how we live today.
